Four Incircles

GeometryCirclesTriangles
What it shows: A triangle with two lines from its top point, making four smaller triangles with a circle in each one.
How to play: Drag the dots, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Watch the two wider circles when the two outer circles become the same size.
Look for the math

Move the four dots and all six circles change. Yet the moment the two outside small circles are the same size, the two middle circles are too — and that is no coincidence.

The five circles

The top point A is joined to four points on one straight line: B, C, D, E in that order. The two inner lines AC and AD are cevians. Each triangle has an incircle: the three small ones in ABC, ACD, ADE (level 1), the two wider ones in ABD, ACE (level 2), and the one in the whole triangle ABE (level 3). The picture shows the level-2 and level-3 circles only when the outer level-1 circles match, just as the Java applet did. Its own test allows a one-pixel difference, because the dots are dragged by hand.

What the page claims

The cut-the-knot page states the Five Incircles Theorem of J. B. Tabov: the incircles of ABC and ADE are equal if and only if those of ABD and ACE are equal. It also gives Demir's weaker statement (B): if ABC, ACD and ADE all have equal incircles, then the level-2 circles match. (B) asks for more, so it says less. This is the claim tested here: over grids of exact configurations and thousands of random fans, the two equalities always hold together, and (B) follows. The live page still embeds the Java applet FourIncircles, so the original itself was available; no archive was needed.

Why the two pairs match

Drop a perpendicular from A to the base and call its length h. For a base point X, write g(X) = (AX + signed distance of X from the foot) / h. A short calculation with the semiperimeter gives

r(A, X, Y) = h/2 × (1 − g(X)/g(Y))

So the outer level-1 circles match exactly when g(B)/g(C) = g(D)/g(E), that is when g(C)g(D) − g(B)g(E) = 0. The level-2 circles match when g(B)/g(D) = g(C)/g(E), which is the very same numerator. Equally, if the three level-1 circles match, the g values form a geometric progression g, gq, gq², gq³, so every circle spanning k gaps has radius h/2 × (1 − q−k) whatever k is. The page's semiperimeter equations (1)–(3) say the same thing; the logic test checks their algebra directly.

A different four-incircles page

The applet called FourIncirclesInTriangle belongs to another cut-the-knot page: a sangaku in an equilateral triangle with three equal-angle lines and the answer l = x(√21 − 3)/4 for the inner side. That is not this picture: here the big triangle need not be equilateral and there are only two cevians, with an if-and-only-if about circle radii. Two small deviations are worth naming. Dragging C or D here slides its neighbour along too, keeping the gap CD fixed; the applet did that and the theorem does not need it. The Make outer circles match button is a modern convenience, not an applet control: it places the dots at a geometric progression so you can see the finished picture at once.

Try Make outer circles match, then move A: all the circles change, but the two pairs still match. Then press New diagram and chase the match by dragging C alone.
